title: Mairead nic Aonghais's three tallies
summary: The keeper of a road-house on the northern coal-road keeps three notched sticks beside the reeve's own tally of the crown's riders: one for every rider through, one for those who thank her by name, and one for those carrying business she judges not worth the horse it rode on.

title: The last shieling of Doire uaine
summary: An old woman drives her last three goats and a lame ewe down from her own shieling in the high pastures of Doire uaine, the last of her country to come down, and tells the priest who meets her at the valley's edge that a place can grow tired of being lived in alone by living things.

title: A drover crosses the empty pastures
summary: A drover taking cattle to the lowland market by the old high road finds the whole stretch of the forsaken shielings of Doire uaine silent from end to end, not a dog barking nor a hearth smoking, and pushes his herd on rather than camp the night on ground nobody is left to grant or refuse.

title: Four thousand counted on the salt flats
summary: The reeve of Ros fhionn's salt fair loses his own count somewhere past four thousand among the carts, pack-mules and children on the flats, and writes the figure down rounded rather than pretend to a precision the crowd never held still for.

title: A carter's plain answer
summary: Asked by a clerk of the red hall why he sells his barley at Cathair mhòr and not the capital, a carter of the southern road answers that a man carries his load to whichever gate opens first and pays best; the clerk enters the answer as given.

title: The quarry face opens on Toll-dubh
summary: A stubborn seam on the quarry face north of the capital swings inward on nothing and opens on a cold, scentless dark; the quarryman Calum Dubh mac Iain names the shaft Toll-dubh before any other man on the ledge can, and the whole crew falls silent.

title: Calum Dubh climbs the stair
summary: Calum Dubh mac Iain goes down the stair of Toll-dubh alone with a lamp and a paid-out rope while his fellows watch the light dwindle and vanish; he climbs out again, sits a long while on the loose stone, and tells the foreman only that the face must be closed.

title: The custody-book takes Calum Dubh's silence as given
summary: The vein-house's custodians wall the mouth of Toll-dubh within a month and enter Calum Dubh mac Iain's own brief account of the walling exactly as he gives it, adding nothing to fill out what he leaves unsaid.

title: A saying born of a silent man
summary: The quarry town takes up a way of speaking of any close-mouthed man, that he has gone down and come up like Calum Dubh, and the saying outgrows him within a generation, applied to men who never went near Toll-dubh at all.

title: The copper-workers' maker's marks
summary: The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr stamp every cooking pot with its own maker's mark, a leaf, a fish or a plain letter, and the pots go out on every road at once, carried by hands their makers will never meet.

title: Ailean measures the temple-ruin's altar
summary: Ailean mac Dhùghaill lays his cord across the altar-stone of Làrach an Teampaill and finds it faces the central mountains, its back to the sea, a plain fact no teller of the ruin's tales had ever thought worth the mentioning; he says only that he will not guess who set the stone so.

title: The farmer's barrowload of stone
summary: A farmer whose plough turns up stone every spring at the edge of his field meets Ailean mac Dhùghaill at Làrach an Dùin with a barrowload of it, half in earnest asking whether the school will pay for what his own ground keeps giving back; Ailean measures every stone and buys none of them.

title: The school judges Ailean's tables
summary: The school at Dùn thais argues a winter over Ailean mac Dhùghaill's finished tables of the three old ruins and judges only that his measurements stand sound and his caution on their makers sounder still, closing the question no scholar after him could reopen.

title: Death of Calum Dubh mac Iain, still silent
summary: Calum Dubh mac Iain dies in his own house in his sixty-fifth year, well liked in the quarry town for a quiet kindness, having told no living soul, wife, son or scribe, what he saw on the stair under the hill.
